units.translation: 16 Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) ἀχαιϊνέα: the deer. Apollonius in Book 4 of the Argonautica: IV 175. From the city Achaea, in which there are species of large deer. Thus Horus in On Ethnic Names. cf. W 89 Eustathius 711, 42. cf. W 62 Hesychius σπαθίνης
17 ἀχ. λεγόμενοι in HF; lacuna indicated by W 63 σπαθῖναι Nauck : επαθιναῖοι in L : -αία (καλεῖται) in P
176-77. βεβρίθει λήνεσσιν: with wool, whence also the wool-carders
19 Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) ληνέων: IV 173. λῆνος means wool, and λίνον means linen.
19 ἐρίοις in LgGgSm

are called the combers. Many have said the fleece was golden, whom Apollonius followed. But Simonides (fr. 21 B. III 396) says it was sometimes white, sometimes purple, and Dionysius of Mytilene (32 fr. 2a J.) says it was a man, the tutor of Phrixus, named Crius.
1 sch. 1146/48 sch. Eur. Med. 5 Tzetz. Chil. I 431 (cf. W 67)
181. ἀφασσόμενος: touching, handling. LgP
182. νοσφίσσεται: will deprive. LgP
190. μηκέτι νῦν χάζεσθε: withdraw and take thought for the return to your homeland. But some write φράζεσθε.
3 sch. I 256/59 with similar passages
191-93. ἤδη γὰρ χρειώ: For the need, he says, for the sake of which we undertook this difficult voyage, has been easily accomplished by the counsels of the maiden.

200-02a. ἑζόμενος πηδοῖσι: with the flat parts of the oars; by which he indicates the oars from a part. For the flat part of the oar is called πηδόν; Theophrastus (Hist. plant. V 7, 6) says πηδόν is a kind of wood.
12 sch. η 328 Apoll. Lex. Hom. 131, 15 B. Hesychius πῆδος. πηδῷ Eustathius 613, 9. 1582, 23
b. And the half of you, armed, ward off the attackers. He has called the shields ἔχμα βολάων. Lm (P)
c. θοόν: instead of the adverb θοῶς. Lg (P)
213. περίπυστος: renowned. LgP
214-15. ἐς δ’ ἀγορὴν ἀγέροντο: they gathered for battle. And he says: just as it is not possible to predict the waves of the sea in a storm, so too the multitude of the armed Colchians. L
218. 〈παρεμέτρεον:〉 they sailed past. Lg
22 perhaps παρέθεον
223-30a. πεύκην περιμήκεα: the torch, as if about to burn the ship.

Apollonius says that Aeetes returned without success with his chariot driven by Absyrtus, but Dionysius of Miletus (32 fr. 10b J.) says that Aeetes, overtaking the ship, when the nobles were drawn up for battle, killed Iphis the Argive, brother of Eurystheus, and lost many himself. Pherecydes in Book 7 (3 fr. 32a J.) says that Medea took him when he was small
